importance_rationale: The candidate is the famous fermion sign problem at full source generality, and the formulation alignment is verified as equivalent: the canonical statement matches the authoritative Troyer & Wiese (PRL 94, 170201) formulation verbatim, with the Dornheim lead (arXiv:2104.10032) restating the same exponential-cost barrier without narrowing it. No scoped variant is being approved under the famous name; scope text contains only intrinsic assumptions from the source formulation (equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo, quantum-degenerate fermions, no model or temperature restriction). The known NP-hardness is correctly retained as context bounding what a generic solution would imply rather than as a resolution of the question. Resolution in either direction would materially change computational many-body physics, so this proceeds to the later-literature Research audit as high importance.
scientific_significance_rationale: A positive resolution would deliver an unbiased, numerically exact polynomial-cost method for thermal properties of correlated fermions, directly changing the capability frontier for warm dense matter, quantum chemistry, and correlated electron systems that are currently blocked by the exponential wall S = exp(-beta N Delta f). A negative resolution extending the known general-case NP-hardness to the stated equilibrium Monte Carlo setting would convert a widely believed practical barrier into a settled fundamental limit, redirecting the field's method-development decisions toward controlled approximations. Held back from 10 only because the most probable outcome is a hardness confirmation of a limit the community already treats as near-certain; even that outcome is a decisive bound, and a construction would be field-transforming.
expected_result: A final submission resolves the source question in one of two committed forms. Either (a) a rigorous impossibility or conditional-hardness theorem establishing that no equilibrium many-body Monte Carlo method can compute thermal properties of general quantum-degenerate fermionic systems with cost sub-exponential in particle number N and inverse temperature beta, stating its assumptions and complexity-theoretic hypotheses explicitly; or (b) a fully specified method accompanied by a correctness argument and a demonstrated, independently checkable sub-exponential cost scaling in N and beta on quantum-degenerate fermionic systems in the general setting, with error bars and systematics documented so the scaling claim, not merely accuracy at one size, is the submitted claim. A method valid only on sign-problem-free subclasses does not constitute the expected result, since the source question commits to the general fermionic setting.
verification_standard: The submission is checked against the original source-faithful question: does an equilibrium Monte Carlo method exist that computes thermal properties of quantum-degenerate fermionic systems at cost not growing exponentially in N and beta? Branch (a): a hardness or impossibility proof passes if its stated assumptions are explicit, its reduction or argument is valid under independent derivation review, and its conclusion covers the general fermionic equilibrium setting rather than an isolated model class already known to Troyer-Wiese. Branch (b): a constructed method passes if (i) its correctness argument for fermionic thermal expectation values is sound, and (ii) its cost model or measured cost, checked by independent replay of the pinned protocol with documented error bars and systematics across increasing N and beta, exhibits sub-exponential scaling on quantum-degenerate fermionic systems not restricted to a sign-problem-free special case. A submission passes exactly when one branch withstands this scrutiny; presenting a special-case construction as the general answer fails.
verification_difficulty_rationale: This result genuinely answers the source question because both acceptance branches settle the existence question the sources pose; the residual limit is that a hardness branch may be conditional on standard complexity hypotheses, which the contract requires to be stated, not discharged. Taking the cheapest sound branch of the either-or contract does not help much: neither branch yields a finite witness. A construction's scaling claim is asymptotic in N and beta, so no finite simulation suite certifies it — replay validates consistency, but the load-bearing claim is the correctness-and-scaling argument itself, a connected derivation the Reviewer must reconstruct, including that the cost model honestly counts all sampling effort (the 1/sqrt(N_MC) compensation noted in the source) and that no exponential factor hides in preprocessing or ensemble choice. A hardness proof is likewise a novel, connected derivation whose reduction must be checked step by step, with nontrivial specification-fidelity work to confirm the formalized computational task faithfully encodes equilibrium fermionic Monte Carlo. The load-bearing items a Reviewer must inspect are: the correctness reduction or error analysis, the explicit cost accounting in N and beta, the generality of the fermionic setting relative to the Troyer-Wiese special cases, and any complexity hypotheses. This is a long, novel chain with substantial specification reconstruction: score 8.
